analysis.one_liner: Lets doctors who own hospitals again refer their Medicare patients to those hospitals.
analysis.headline: A bill to lift the limits on doctor-owned hospital self-referrals never left the Senate Finance Committee and died without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the Affordable Care Act rules that stop doctors from sending their Medicare patients to hospitals they own a piece of, as long as those hospitals were built or expanded after 2010. Those rules exist because studies and the law's sponsors found that doctors who profit from a hospital order more tests and admissions there, raising costs for Medicare. The bill would once again allow doctors to own and self-refer to new hospitals.
analysis.who_benefits: Physician investors who want to build, expand, or hold stakes in hospitals that treat Medicare patients. Repealing the limits would let them profit again from referring their own patients to facilities they own, a practice the ACA shut off for new hospitals.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals sections 6001 and 10601 of the Affordable Care Act and section 1106 of the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act, restoring Medicare rules as if those limits on physician-owned hospital self-referral had never been written [S3][S2].
Supporters say physician-owned hospitals can add beds, operating rooms, and specialized services in growing communities, and the bill's title frames it as expanding patient access to care [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare and its taxpayers, plus patients' out-of-pocket costs. When doctors earn money by referring patients to a hospital they own, research that led to the 2010 restrictions showed higher admission, testing, and imaging rates — costs that flow to Medicare and patients.

drawbacks.text: Self-referral restores a financial conflict of interest: doctors deciding whether a patient needs a hospital admission or scan would also profit from that decision, which is why the ACA Congress shut off self-referral for new physician-owned hospitals [S2][S3].

Restricting new physician-owned hospitals can genuinely limit competition and hospital capacity in fast-growing areas; an honest supporter would acknowledge the bill trades that access argument for re-opening a conflict-of-interest channel [S1].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain is more physician-owned hospital capacity in some communities; the cost is reintroducing a referral-for-profit arrangement that Medicare pays for through higher utilization. On balance the bill's main effect is a revenue opening for physician investors, paid for in the Medicare program and patient bills.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2022 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Lankford introduced the bill with 11 Republican cosponsors on May 3, 2022 [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The committee held no markup and the full Senate never voted on it before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The limits on doctor self-referral stay in place for new physician-owned hospitals, so Medicare keeps the protections and physician investors did not get the revenue opening they sought. Nobody moved the bill, so the outcome is mostly a default rather than a contested defeat.

for.name: Sen. James Lankford
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oklahoma and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the ACA limits on physician-owned hospital self-referral and sought cosponsors.

for.name: 11 of 50 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a Republican-only base of support.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: The Finance Committee, which he chaired, took no action after the bill was referred — no markup, no vote, and it never reached the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat joined, and the Democratic-chaired Finance Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Physician-owned hospitals and their physician investors
industries.note: Repeal would let doctors again own new hospitals and refer their own Medicare patients there, reopening a revenue channel the ACA closed because self-referral drives higher admissions and imaging. The doctors' gain comes through Medicare payments and patient utilization.

Physician-owned specialist hospitals would siphon well-insured surgical and imaging cases away from community hospitals, which historically backed the self-referral limits. Their interest in the bill runs alongside patients' interest in referral decisions made without owner profit.
